meta.title: WW1 — Verdun to the first tanks (example chapter)

scenes.beat: By the end of 1915, the man who had replaced Moltke,

elements.name: General Erich von Falkenhayn
elements.role: Chief of the German General Staff, 1914-16

scenes.beat: General Erich von Falkenhayn, had a problem with no obvious answer.
Attacks on the Western Front gained almost nothing and cost enormous numbers of men.
So he went looking for a different kind of battle.

elements.title: FALKENHAYN — AS HE WROTE AFTER THE WAR

scenes.beat: According to the memoirs he wrote after the war,
his idea was that France could still be beaten without a breakthrough,
if the French army could be made to lose enough men.
Pick a place the French could not afford to give up, and let German heavy guns do the killing.
The place he picked was Verdun, a fortress town on the river Meuse.
The attack began in February 1916.
It became the longest battle of the war, lasting about three hundred days.
And the arithmetic never worked the way the plan said it would.
One modern calculation puts French casualties at around three hundred and seventy-seven thousand and German casualties at around three hundred and thirty-seven
That's roughly seventy thousand men a month, for most of a year, on the hills north of one town.
The army that was supposed to bleed was the German army, too.
And while Verdun went on, the other side opened two more doors.
In June, the Russian general Aleksei Brusilov
attacked on a wide front in the east and smashed the Austro-Hungarian armies,
inflicting losses they would never really recover from.
Germany had to send divisions east to hold its ally up,
and Romania was encouraged to join the war on the Allied side.
Then, on the 1st of July, the British and French attacked on the Somme.
On its first day, the British army suffered fifty-seven thousand four hundred and seventy casualties,
including nineteen thousand two hundred and forty killed.

elements.text: WORST DAY IN BRITISH ARMY HISTORY

scenes.beat: It's still the worst day in the history of the British Army.
But the battle went on for a hundred and forty-one days,
and the Germans facing it bled as well.
In September, the first tanks in history crawled into action there.
